chapter.title: Waves
chapter.description: Study the propagation of disturbances, mechanical waves, transverse and longitudinal waves, progressive waves, wave speed, superposition, reflection, standing waves, normal modes and beats.

topics.title: What is a Wave?
topics.content: A wave is a moving disturbance that propagates from one point to another without the actual physical transfer or flow of matter as a whole.

topics.title: Energy Transfer
topics.content: Waves transport energy and propagate information from one point to another.

topics.title: Mechanical Waves
topics.content: Mechanical waves require a material medium for propagation. Examples include waves on a string, water waves, sound waves and seismic waves.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Waves
topics.content: Electromagnetic waves do not necessarily require a medium and can propagate through vacuum. Examples include light, radio waves and X-rays.

topics.title: Matter Waves
topics.content: Matter waves are associated with particles such as electrons, protons, neutrons, atoms and molecules.

topics.title: Wave Propagation in a Medium
topics.content: A disturbance propagates through coupled oscillating elements of a medium. Elastic forces transmit the disturbance from one element to another.

topics.title: Transverse Waves
topics.definition: The constituents of the medium oscillate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.

topics.title: Longitudinal Waves
topics.definition: The constituents of the medium oscillate along the direction of wave propagation.

topics.title: Compressions and Rarefactions
topics.content: Longitudinal sound waves propagate through successive compressions and rarefactions of the medium.

topics.title: Progressive Waves
topics.definition: A travelling or progressive wave moves from one part of the medium to another while the medium as a whole does not move with the wave.

topics.title: Propagation in Different Media
topics.content: Transverse waves require a medium capable of sustaining shear stress, whereas longitudinal waves can propagate in elastic solids, liquids and gases.

topics.title: Water Waves
topics.content: Water waves involve complicated particle motion and can contain both transverse and longitudinal components.

sections.title: Displacement Relation in a Progressive Wave

topics.title: Wave Function
topics.description: A sinusoidal travelling wave propagating in the positive x-direction.

topics.title: Amplitude
topics.definition: Maximum displacement of the constituents of the medium from their equilibrium position.

topics.title: Phase
topics.definition: The phase determines the displacement of the wave at a particular position and instant.

topics.title: Initial Phase
topics.definition: The phase at x = 0 and t = 0.

topics.title: Wavelength
topics.definition: The minimum distance between two points having the same phase.

sections.title: The Speed of a Travelling Wave

topics.title: Physical Meaning
topics.content: During one complete oscillation of a constituent of the medium, the wave pattern travels a distance equal to one wavelength.

topics.title: Dependence of Wave Speed
topics.content: The speed of a mechanical wave depends on the inertial and elastic properties of the medium.

subsections.title: Speed of a Transverse Wave on a Stretched String
subsections.importantPoint: The speed depends on the properties of the string and does not depend on the wavelength or frequency of the wave itself.

sections.title: The Principle of Superposition of Waves

topics.title: Superposition Principle
topics.definition: When two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements.

topics.title: Interference
topics.content: The principle of superposition is fundamental to the phenomenon of interference.

topics.title: Reflection at a Rigid Boundary
topics.content: A travelling wave or pulse suffers a phase change of π on reflection at a rigid boundary.

topics.title: Reflection at an Open Boundary
topics.content: At a completely free boundary, the reflected pulse has the same phase as the incident pulse, assuming no energy dissipation.

topics.title: Echo
topics.content: Echo is an example of reflection by a rigid boundary.

topics.title: Standing Wave Formation
topics.description: Produced by superposition of two waves of equal amplitude and wavelength travelling in opposite directions.

topics.title: Nodes
topics.definition: Points where the amplitude is zero and there is no motion.

topics.title: Antinodes
topics.definition: Points where the amplitude is maximum.

topics.title: Harmonics
topics.content: n = 1 is the fundamental or first harmonic, n = 2 is the second harmonic, n = 3 is the third harmonic, and so on.

topics.title: Air Column Closed at One End
topics.content: Only odd harmonics occur.

topics.title: Open Pipe
topics.content: For an air column open at both ends, both ends are antinodes and all harmonics can occur.

topics.title: Resonance
topics.content: A system shows resonance when the external frequency is close to one of its natural frequencies.

example.title: Resonance in an Open Pipe
example.result: The source resonates with the second harmonic of the open pipe.

topics.title: Formation of Beats
topics.definition: Beats arise when two waves having slightly different frequencies and comparable amplitudes are superposed.

topics.title: Nature of Beats
topics.content: The sound intensity periodically increases and decreases, producing audible waxing and waning.

summary: Mechanical waves exist in material media.
Transverse waves have particle oscillations perpendicular to propagation.
Longitudinal waves have particle oscillations parallel to propagation.
A progressive wave moves from one point of a medium to another.
A sinusoidal wave travelling in the positive x-direction is represented by y(x,t) = a sin(kx - ωt + φ).
Wavelength is the distance between consecutive points having the same phase.
Wave speed v = ω/k = λ/T = λν.
Speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string is v = √(T/μ).
Sound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves and can propagate through solids, liquids and gases.
The speed of a longitudinal wave is v = √(B/ρ).
The principle of superposition states that resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of individual displacements.
Reflection at a rigid boundary produces a phase change of π.
Standing waves contain nodes and antinodes.
A string fixed at both ends has frequencies νn = nv/(2L).
An air column closed at one end supports odd harmonics.
Beats occur when two waves of slightly different frequencies are superposed.
pointsToPonder: A wave is not motion of matter as a whole in a medium.
Energy, rather than matter, is transferred from one point to another.
Mechanical wave energy transfer occurs through elastic coupling between neighbouring oscillating parts.
Transverse waves require a medium with shear elasticity.
Longitudinal waves can propagate in solids, liquids and gases.
In a harmonic progressive wave, particles have the same amplitude but different phases.
In a stationary wave, particles between two nodes have the same phase but different amplitudes.
The speed of a mechanical wave in a medium depends on the elastic and inertial properties of the medium.
